content.text:
I couldn't find the UPS, but I think I know why.

Windows doesn't see any APC device on this computer. APC devices identify themselves to Windows with ID `VID_051D`, and nothing with that ID is connected. The only thing plugged in during the last few minutes was a **USB-to-Ethernet adapter**, at 12:07, and it shows no network link.

That suggests a cable mix-up that's easy to make with APC units. On many APC models, the "USB" data port on the UPS looks like an **Ethernet jack**. It needs APC's special cable, which has a jack-shaped plug on one end and a normal USB plug on the other (APC part 940-0127). A regular network cable into a USB-Ethernet adapter won't work. The beep you heard was probably just the UPS reacting to something being plugged into its port.

Can you check two things?

1. **Which cable is it?** Look at the end that goes into the UPS.
   - If it's a normal USB plug into a USB port on the UPS, try a different USB port on the computer. Avoid hubs and the front-panel ports if you can.
   - If it's a jack-shaped plug, look at the other end. If that's also jack-shaped and goes into the USB-Ethernet adapter, that's a network cable, and it won't work for this. You need the APC cable. It often came in the UPS box, and replacements cost about $15–20. Unplug the network cable from the UPS for now.
2. **What's the model on the UPS label?** That tells me exactly which cable and port it uses.

As soon as Windows sees it, I'll be able to find it, and it should show up as a "HID UPS Battery".

content.text:
That setup won't work. The pieces fit physically, but they speak different languages:

- The UPS's data port carries **USB signals** wired into a jack-shaped socket, which is APC's own design.
- A **USB-to-Ethernet adapter** is a network card. It expects a real network on the other end, so the computer only ever sees "network cable unplugged."

Unplug the Ethernet cable from the UPS. A normal network cable in that port is unlikely to cause damage, but it isn't what the port is meant for.

**What you need:** APC's USB data cable, part **940-0127**. It has a jack-shaped plug on one end and a regular USB plug on the other.

1. Check the UPS box first; it usually comes included.
2. If you don't have it, a genuine APC or a well-reviewed "940-0127B/E compatible" cable costs about $10–20. Generic "RJ45-to-USB" console cables for network switches won't work, because they're wired differently.

Once it's plugged straight into a USB port on the computer, Windows will show it as a battery, and I can read its wattage.

The UPS piece can be added later, so it doesn't need to hold up the rest. I can build the dashboard on Vercel with the Enphase data and leave the UPS spot ready. Two answers from before would let me start:

1. **Is this computer usually on?** The collector that reads the gateway and the UPS would run here.
2. **Can you log in to enlighten.enphaseenergy.com?** That's needed for the local gateway token.

--- title: Route Handlers nav_title: Route Handlers description: Create custom request handlers with Next.js Route Handlers using the Web Request and Response APIs. related: title: API Reference description: Learn more about Route Handlers links: - app/api-reference/file-conventions/route - app/guides/backend-for-frontend --- ## Route Handlers Route Handlers allow you to create custom request handlers for a given route using the Web [Request](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Request) and [Response](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Response) APIs. > **Good to know**: Route Handlers are only available inside the `app` directory. They are the equivalent of [API Routes](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/api-routes) inside the `pages` directory meaning you **do not** need to use API Routes and Route Handlers together. ### Convention Route Handlers are defined in a [`route.js|ts` file](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route) inside the `app` directory: ```ts filename="app/api/route.ts" switcher export async function GET(request: Request) {} ``` ```js filename="app/api/route.js" switcher export async function GET(request) {} ``` Route Handlers can be nested anywhere inside the `app` directory, similar to `page.js` and `layout.js`. But there **cannot** be a `route.js` file at the same route segment level as `page.js`. ### Supported HTTP Methods The following [HTTP methods](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods) are supported: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, and `OPTIONS`. If an unsupported method is called, Next.js will return a `405 Method Not Allowed` response. ### Extended `NextRequest` and `NextResponse` APIs In addition to supporting the native [Request](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Request) and [Response](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Response) APIs, Next.js extends them with [`NextRequest`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-request) and [`NextResponse`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response) to provide convenient helpers for advanced use cases. ### Caching Route Handlers are not cached by default. You can, however, opt into caching for `GET` methods. Other supported HTTP methods are **not** cached. To cache a `GET` method, use a [route config option](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components#dynamic) such as `export const dynamic = 'force-static'` in your Route Handler file. ```ts filename="app/items/route.ts" switcher export const dynamic = 'force-static' export async function GET() { const res = await fetch('https://data.mongodb-api.com/...', { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'API-Key': process.env.DATA_API_KEY, }, }) const data = await res.json() return Response.json({ data }) } ``` ```js filename="app/items/route.js" switcher export const dynamic = 'force-static' export async function GET() { const res = await fetch('https://data.mongodb-api.com/...', { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'API-Key': process.env.DATA_API_KEY, }, }) const data = await res.json() return Response.json({ data }) } ``` > **Good to know**: Other supported HTTP methods are **not** cached, even if they are placed alongside a `GET` method that is cached, in the same file. #### With Cache Components When [Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) is enabled, `GET` Route Handlers follow the same model as normal UI routes in your application. They run at request time by default, can be prerendered when they don't access uncached or runtime data, and you can use `use cache` to include uncached data in the static response. **Static example** - doesn't access uncached or runtime data, so it will be prerendered at build time: ```tsx filename="app/api/project-info/route.ts" export async function GET() { return Response.json({ projectName: 'Next.js', }) } ``` **Dynamic example** - accesses non-deterministic operations. During the build, prerendering stops when `Math.random()` is called, deferring to request-time rendering: ```tsx filename="app/api/random-number/route.ts" export async function GET() { return Response.json({ randomNumber: Math.random(), }) } ``` **Runtime data example** - accesses request-specific data. Prerendering terminates when runtime APIs like `headers()` are called: ```tsx filename="app/api/user-agent/route.ts" import { headers } from 'next/headers' export async function GET() { const headersList = await headers() const userAgent = headersList.get('user-agent') return Response.json({ userAgent }) } ``` > **Good to know**: Prerendering stops if the `GET` handler accesses network requests, database queries, async file system operations, request object properties (like `req.url`, `request.headers`, `request.cookies`, `request.body`), runtime APIs like [`cookies()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies), [`headers()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/headers), [`connection()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/connection), or non-deterministic operations. **Cached example** - accesses uncached data (database query) but caches it with `use cache`, allowing it to be included in the prerendered response: ```tsx filename="app/api/products/route.ts" import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' export async function GET() { const products = await getProducts() return Response.json(products) } async function getProducts() { 'use cache' cacheLife('hours') return await db.query('SELECT * FROM products') } ``` > **Good to know**: `use cache` cannot be used directly inside a Route Handler body; extract it to a helper function. Cached responses revalidate according to `cacheLife` when a new request arrives. ### Special Route Handlers Special Route Handlers like [`sitemap.ts`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/sitemap), [`opengraph-image.tsx`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/opengraph-image), and [`icon.tsx`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/app-icons), and other [metadata files](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata) remain static by default unless they use Request-time APIs or dynamic config options. ### Route Resolution You can consider a `route` the lowest level routing primitive. - They **do not** participate in layouts or client-side navigations like `page`. - There **cannot** be a `route.js` file at the same route as `page.js`. | Page | Route | Result | | -------------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------- | | `app/page.js` | `app/route.js` | Conflict | | `app/page.js` | `app/api/route.js` | Valid | | `app/[user]/page.js` | `app/api/route.js` | Valid | Each `route.js` or `page.js` file takes over all HTTP verbs for that route. ```ts filename="app/page.ts" switcher export default function Page() { return

Hello, Next.js!

} // Conflict // `app/route.ts` export async function POST(request: Request) {} ``` ```js filename="app/page.js" switcher export default function Page() { return

Hello, Next.js!

} // Conflict // `app/route.js` export async function POST(request) {} ``` Read more about how Route Handlers [complement your frontend application](/docs/app/guides/backend-for-frontend), or explore the Route Handlers [API Reference](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route). ### Route Context Helper In TypeScript, you can type the `context` parameter for Route Handlers with the globally available [`RouteContext`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route#route-context-helper) helper: ```ts filename="app/users/[id]/route.ts" switcher import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server' export async function GET(_req: NextRequest, ctx: RouteContext<'/users/[id]'>) { const { id } = await ctx.params return Response.json({ id }) } ``` > **Good to know** after.md cacheLife.md cacheTag.md catchError.md connection.md cookies.md draft-mode.md fetch.md forbidden.md generate-image-metadata.md generate-metadata.md generate-sitemaps.md generate-static-params.md generate-viewport.md headers.md image-response.md index.md io.md next-request.md next-response.md next-root-params.md not-found.md permanentRedirect.md redirect.md refresh.md revalidatePath.md revalidateTag.md unauthorized.md unstable_cache.md unstable_noStore.md unstable_rethrow.md updateTag.md use-link-status.md use-offline.md use-params.md use-pathname.md use-report-web-vitals.md use-router.md use-search-params.md use-selected-layout-segment.md

content.text:
That's expected: the gateway token doesn't come from the developer portal. Enphase has three separate logins, and the token comes from one you haven't used yet:

| Site | Login | What it's for |
|---|---|---|
| developer-v4.enphase.com | Your **developer** account | The cloud API key and client ID/secret, which we'll use later for history |
| enlighten.enphaseenergy.com / the Enphase app | Your **homeowner** account | Viewing your system |
| **entrez.enphaseenergy.com** | Your **homeowner** account, the same one as the app | **← the gateway token comes from here** |

Your developer account may not be able to see your system at all, so use your **homeowner** login here:

1. Open **https://entrez.enphaseenergy.com** in a new tab. If it signs you in automatically as the developer account, log out first or use a private window.
2. Log in with the **email and password you use in the Enphase phone app**.
3. On the page that loads:
   - Under **Select System**, start typing your system's name, as it appears at the top of the Enphase app, and choose it.
   - Under **Select Gateway**, choose serial **`122025062156`**.
   - Click **Create access token** (it may say "Generate Access Token").
4. Copy the long token, paste it after `GATEWAY_TOKEN=` in `solar-dashboard\collector\.env`, and save.

If you're asked whether you're an owner or an installer, choose **owner**. Owner tokens last 12 months; installer tokens expire after 12 hours.

If you get stuck, tell me what you see on the page after logging in.

Sources:
- [evcc docs: Enphase IQ Gateway](https://docs.evcc.io/en/nightly/meters/enphase-iq-gateway)
- [Sourceful Energy help: Enphase](https://intercom.help/sourceful-energy/en/articles/11487027-enphase)

---
name: solar-dashboard-project
description: Enphase solar dashboard (Codestuff/solar-dashboard) — Next.js 16 on Vercel + local collector; hardware facts and constraints
metadata:
  type: project
---

Custom Enphase dashboard started 2026-10-04 in `Codestuff/solar-dashboard` (Next.js 16 app for Vercel + `collector/collector.mjs` run on the home PC).

- IQ Gateway at 192.168.1.166 (envoy.local), firmware D8.3, owner token in `collector/.env` (expires 2027-10-04 — renew at entrez.enphaseenergy.com with the *homeowner* login, not the developer account).
- 23 microinverters; 2 silent (serials ending 1110 since 2024-07-17, 3131 since 2026-07-23). No batteries.
- Net-consumption meter is **disabled** → no real home-usage/grid data; total-consumption just echoes production. whToday mirrors whLifetime on D8, so "today" must come from lifetime-counter baselines.
- Enphase cloud API is on the free Watt plan: 1000 hits/month, 10/min, site-level only (per-panel needs $249/mo plan) — so live/per-panel data comes from the local collector.
- APC UPS for per-device load: user lacks the APC 940-0127 USB cable (tried Ethernet + USB-Ethernet adapter, which can't work). `ups` slot in the payload is a stub until then.
- User wants a "Problems" panel and per-room/device power eventually (discussed circuit monitors / smart plugs).

## Warranty Coverage When Installer Goes Out of Business

Equipment warranties survive when an installer closes, but the installer's warranties do not. Specifically:

- **Equipment Warranty**: Equipment and product warranties issued by the manufacturer (covering defects in panels, inverters, and microinverters) survive with the equipment, not with the company that installed it.

- **Workmanship/Labor Warranty**: Workmanship and labor warranties (typically 10 to 25 years) are issued by your installer and do not survive - in a Chapter 7 liquidation they are gone.

## Enphase's Approach to Orphaned Systems

Enphase will accept claims directly from homeowners and sells Enphase Care directly to homeowners starting at $399, with $0 on-site labor on covered repairs, and states it will send technicians if your installer closed.

Additionally, standard warranty labor is reimbursed to certified installers, and Enphase Care exists to close that gap for homeowners.

## Microinverter Replacement Labor

Enphase microinverters carry a 25-year warranty honored by the manufacturer directly - if your inverter fails within the warranty period, the replacement unit is free, though you pay only for the labor to swap it.

However, labor of the installation comes out of the owner's pocket in standard warranty replacements when an installer is no longer available.

That's common, and your warranty doesn't depend on the installer still being around. **The microinverter warranty comes from Enphase**, and Enphase accepts claims directly from homeowners whose installer has closed. What you lost is the installer's **workmanship and labor** warranty, so the replacement units should be free, but someone has to be paid to put them on the roof.

**What to do:**

1. **Contact Enphase support directly** through enphase.com, under Support / Contact Us. Tell them your installer went out of business and that two microinverters have stopped reporting. Have this ready:

   | | |
   |---|---|
   | Gateway serial | `122025062156` |
   | Failed microinverter | `202015011110`, silent since July 17, 2024 |
   | Failed microinverter | `202101033131`, silent since July 23, 2026 |
   | Part number (both) | `800-00625-r02` |
   | Installed | 2021 |

   Enphase can see your system remotely, so they can confirm the failures themselves.

2. **Ask Enphase about labor.** For homeowners without an installer, Enphase can send its own field technicians or refer you to a certified installer near you. It also sells **Enphase Care**, a homeowner service plan reported to start around $399, which covers on-site labor for repairs. Get a labor quote from a local certified installer before deciding whether the plan is worth it.

3. **While someone's on the roof,** have them look at the **consumption CTs**. Then the same visit can fix the missing home-usage data.

For scale: those two microinverters would make about **0.5 kW at a sunny peak**, or roughly **2–3 kWh on a good day**. That's real money over a year, but not urgent. Your other 21 are working well.

Should I set up the free **Upstash Redis** database on your Vercel account so I can finish the dashboard?

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

content.content:
# Reference palette

This is the **reference instance** of the data-viz method: every parameter the
method needs, filled in with a validated default palette. The rest of the skill
is system-agnostic - **to target your brand, substitute this file's values** and
re-run the validator. Nothing else changes.

## How to use these values

Everything below is plain hex. In an HTML chart, **define the slots you use as
CSS custom properties in a local `<style>` block** at the top of the file, then
reference them by role throughout - so the light/dark values swap in one place,
and the chart body is written against roles rather than raw hex:

```css
.viz-root {
  color-scheme: light;
  --surface-1:      #fcfcfb;   /* chart surface */
  --text-primary:   #0b0b0b;
  --text-secondary: #52514e;
  --series-1:       #2a78d6;   /* categorical slot 1 */
  /* ...only the roles this chart uses */
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:where(:not([data-theme="light"])) .viz-root {
    color-scheme: dark;
    --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
    --text-primary:   #ffffff;
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] .viz-root {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
  --text-primary:   #ffffff;
  --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
  --series-1:       #3987e5;
}
```

Declare the dark values under both scopes as above - the media query covers
the OS setting; the `data-theme` scope covers the viewer's theme toggle,
which must win both ways (the `:not(...)` guard lets a light stamp beat
OS-dark; `:where()` keeps the media block below the toggle scope).

## Categorical palette

Both modes are selected. The dark column is the same eight hues stepped for the
dark surface, not a separate palette:

| Slot | Hue | Light | Dark |
|------|-----|-------|------|
| 1 | blue | `#2a78d6` | `#3987e5` |
| 2 | orange | `#eb6834` | `#d95926` |
| 3 | aqua | `#1baf7a` | `#199e70` |
| 4 | yellow | `#eda100` | `#c98500` |
| 5 | magenta | `#e87ba4` | `#d55181` |
| 6 | green | `#008300` | `#008300` |
| 7 | violet | `#4a3aa7` | `#9085e9` |
| 8 | red | `#e34948` | `#e66767` |

This order passes every hard gate in both modes on the default *adjacent*
pairlist (stacks, bars, lines): worst adjacent CVD Delta E 9.1 light / 8.4 dark
(OKLab ×100, >=8 target), worst adjacent normal-vision Delta E 19.6 light / 19.3
dark (>=15 floor). Under `--pairs all` (scatter, bubble, choropleth, small
multiples) the full eight cannot clear the floors - with all 28 pairs in
play no ordering can (the pairlist no longer depends on order), and
re-stepping is off the table by the documented-palette rule - so those
chart forms carry a series cap: **the first three slots validate all-pairs
in both modes** (worst pair CVD Delta E 9.2 light / 9.4 dark, normal-vision 24.0
light / 20.9 dark - clear of the CVD warn band). Past three, fold to "Other" or
facet: the fourth slot puts yellow and orange on screen
together, and that pair fails the all-pairs floors (normal-vision 13.7
light; CVD 4.8 dark). Three light-mode slots (magenta, yellow, aqua)
sit below 3:1 contrast on the light surface: the **relief rule** applies (ship
visible direct labels or the table view). The dark steps were chosen for the
dark band (OKLCH L ~ 0.48-0.67, >= 3:1 on the dark surface) and validated as a
set. (Ordering history: adopted July 2026 for its more harmonious opening -
the same eight hues and steps as its predecessor, re-ordered, zero hex
changes. The predecessor validated its first FOUR slots all-pairs, with its
dark run in the 6-8 CVD warn band, so secondary encoding was required there;
this order deliberately trades that fourth slot - yellow now sits beside orange -
for better-looking leading colors. Revisit the trade if yellow<->orange
confusion shows up in real charts with four or more series; undoing it is a
pure re-order.) When you swap in your own ramps, hold your palette to the full
gate.

The slot **ordering** is the CVD-safety mechanism, not cosmetic - candidate
orderings were enumerated and only those clearing every adjacent gate in both
modes kept (see `color-formula.md` § Themes); this default is one of the
passing orders, picked among them for its opening colors. When you swap in
your brand's hues, do the same: run the validator on candidate orderings and
choose only among the passing ones.

## Sequential hue

Default single hue: **blue**, light->dark. When two sequential contexts appear at
once, the second takes the next categorical slot's hue (orange), each as its own
one-hue ramp.

| step | hex | step | hex | step | hex | step | hex |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | `#cde2fb` | 250 | `#86b6ef` | 400 | `#3987e5` | 550 | `#1c5cab` |
| 150 | `#b7d3f6` | 300 | `#6da7ec` | 450 | `#2a78d6` | 600 | `#184f95` |

title: proxy.js
description: API reference for the proxy.js file.
related:
  title: Learn more about Proxy
  links:
    - app/api-reference/functions/next-request
    - app/api-reference/functions/next-response
---
> **Note**: The `middleware` file convention is deprecated and has been renamed to `proxy`. See [Migration to Proxy](#migration-to-proxy) for more details.
The `proxy.js|ts` file is used to write [Proxy](/docs/app/getting-started/proxy) and run code on the server before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.
Proxy executes before routes are rendered. It's particularly useful for implementing custom server-side logic like authentication, logging, or handling redirects.
> **Good to know**:
>
> Proxy is meant to be invoked separately of your render code and in optimized cases deployed to your CDN for fast redirect/rewrite handling, you should not attempt relying on shared modules or globals.
>
> To pass information from Proxy to your application, use [headers](#setting-headers), [cookies](#using-cookies), [rewrites](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#rewrite), [redirects](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#redirect), or the URL.
Create a `proxy.ts` (or `.js`) file in the project root, or inside `src` if applicable, so that it is located at the same level as `pages` or `app`.
If you’ve customized [`pageExtensions`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/pageExtensions), for example to `.page.ts` or `.page.js`, name your file `proxy.page.ts` or `proxy.page.js` accordingly.
```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
}
export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*',
}
```
```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
export function proxy(request) {
  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
}
export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*',
}
```
## Exports
### Proxy function
The file must export a single function, either as a default export or named `proxy`. Note that multiple proxy from the same file are not supported.
```js filename="proxy.js"
// Example of default export
export default function proxy(request) {
  // Proxy logic
}
```
### Config object (optional)
Optionally, a config object can be exported alongside the Proxy function. This object includes the [matcher](#matcher) to specify paths where the Proxy applies.
### Matcher
The `matcher` option allows you to target specific paths for the Proxy to run on.
Without a `matcher`, Proxy runs on **every request**, including static files (`_next/static`), image optimizations (`_next/image`), and assets in the `public/` folder. Consider using a [negative match pattern](#negative-matching) to exclude these paths, otherwise auth logic or redirects can unintentionally block CSS, JS, or images from loading.
You can specify paths in several ways:
- For a single path: Directly use a string to define the path, like `'/about'`.
- For multiple paths: Use an array to list multiple paths, such as `matcher: ['/about', '/contact']`, which applies the Proxy to both `/about` and `/contact`.
import type { NextConfig } from "next";

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  /* config options here */
};

export default nextConfig;

content.content:
# Enphase API Token Exchange and Usage

## Authorization Code Exchange Request

**URL:** `https://api.enphaseenergy.com/oauth/token`

**Method:** POST

**Parameters:** The documentation shows this can be passed as query parameters:
- `grant_type=authorization_code`
- `redirect_uri` (must match the original redirect URI)
- `code` (authorization code from homeowner approval)

**Authentication:** Basic auth header with base64-encoded client credentials

Example: `"Authorization: Basic ZjJhNDc5ZjNjNjA2N2YwZDk1MTdjYWRhZTdmMDBiNDc6NTAzNWNhNjRjMTNmNzkzYTdjMWJjYTQzNTU5MWQ1ZWE="`

## Refresh Token Request

**URL:** `https://api.enphaseenergy.com/oauth/token`

**Parameters (query):**
- `grant_type=refresh_token`
- `refresh_token=unique_refresh_token`

**Authentication:** Same basic auth header format as above

## Example API Call

```
GET /api/v4/systems?key=REDACTED HTTP/1.1
Host: api.enphaseenergy.com
Authorization: Bearer unique_access_token
```

## API Reference Links

The page references documentation sections but does not provide direct URLs to comprehensive API reference pages. Navigation mentions:
- `/docs/monitoring_api`
- `/docs/commissioning_api`
- `/docs/vpp_api`

I've done everything I can without you. Two things need your hands, and then I'll deploy:

**1. Approve the free database (one click)**
Open this link and accept Upstash's terms. It's the free tier, and it'll be created on your Vercel account:
👉 https://vercel.com/annavi11arrea1s-projects/~/integrations/accept-terms/upstash?source=cli

**2. Add your keys in Vercel**
Open https://vercel.com/annavi11arrea1s-projects/solar-dashboard/settings/environment-variables and add these, ticking **Production** (and Preview if you like):

| Name | Value |
|---|---|
| `ENPHASE_API_KEY` | API key from your developer portal app |
| `ENPHASE_CLIENT_ID` | Client ID from the same app |
| `ENPHASE_CLIENT_SECRET` | Client secret from the same app |
| `DASHBOARD_PASSWORD` | A password you choose. Your dashboard shows when you're producing power and when you're home, so I've kept it private. |

Typing them into Vercel means the keys never pass through this chat. The secrets the collector and daily job use are already generated and stored.

**When you said you have the microinverters:** do you mean you have **spare replacement units**? If so, that's good news, but swapping them involves working on the roof with live AC wiring, so a solar technician should do it. The new units also have to be added to your gateway afterward, which is normally done with Enphase's installer app. I can explain that part when you get there.

**What's built:**
- **The dashboard page:** production now, today, month and lifetime; a Problems list; today's power curve; a grid of all 23 panels with the two dead ones marked; the last 30 days and 12 months; and impact numbers. Cards for home usage and UPS power fill in once that hardware is connected.
- **A daily Enphase cloud sync:** about 90 of your 1,000 free monthly API calls.
- **The collector:** already tested against your gateway.

Tell me when steps 1 and 2 are done. Then I'll deploy, start the collector, and send you the link.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

# Solar dashboard

Private dashboard for the home Enphase system: https://solar-dashboard-coral.vercel.app

```
Home PC ── collector/collector.mjs (every 60 s)
   ├─ IQ Gateway (192.168.1.166, local API, owner token)
   └─ APC UPS (not yet — needs APC USB cable 940-0127)
        │ POST /api/ingest  (Bearer INGEST_SECRET)
        ▼
Vercel (Next.js 16) ── Upstash Redis ── dashboard page (DASHBOARD_PASSWORD)
        ▲
        └─ /api/cron/daily (Vercel Cron, 11:00 UTC) → Enphase cloud API v4
           summary + daily history, ~3 calls/day of the free 1,000/month
```

## Collector

Runs from the Windows scheduled task **Solar Dashboard Collector** (starts at logon, hidden,
logs to `collector/collector.log`).

```sh
node collector/collector.mjs --once --print   # one reading, printed and pushed
node collector/collector.mjs --probe          # dump raw gateway JSON to collector/probe/
```

Config is `collector/.env` (template: `collector/.env.example`). The gateway token expires
yearly — the dashboard's Problems list warns 30 days ahead. Renew at
https://entrez.enphaseenergy.com using the **homeowner** login (not the developer account).

## Vercel environment variables

| Name | What |
|---|---|
| `KV_REST_API_URL`, `KV_REST_API_TOKEN` | Added by the Upstash integration |
| `INGEST_SECRET` | Shared with `collector/.env` |
| `CRON_SECRET` | Sent by Vercel Cron to `/api/cron/daily` |
| `DASHBOARD_PASSWORD` | Login for the dashboard |
| `ENPHASE_API_KEY`, `ENPHASE_CLIENT_ID`, `ENPHASE_CLIENT_SECRET` | Developer portal app |
| `ENPHASE_SYSTEM_ID` | Optional; looked up automatically after connecting |
| `HOME_TIMEZONE` | `America/Chicago` — when "today" starts |

After deploying, open the dashboard and click **Connect Enphase** once to authorize the cloud API.

## Known hardware gaps

- Consumption meter is disabled on the gateway → no home-use / grid data until CTs are installed or enabled.
- Two microinverters (202015011110, 202101033131) have stopped reporting — warranty claim with Enphase.

entries.name: TaskStop
entries.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop

content.text:
Your dashboard is live at **https://solar-dashboard-coral.vercel.app**. Log in with the `DASHBOARD_PASSWORD` you set in Vercel. It's receiving fresh readings from your gateway every minute; the latest showed about 5.7 kW. I checked the page at desktop and phone sizes.

**What's on it:**
- **Now and totals:** current production, plus today, this month and lifetime totals (58.8 MWh).
- **Problems:** both dead microinverters with their full serial numbers and how long they've been silent (809 days and 73 days). It also says home usage isn't measured, and it will warn you about a stale collector, a panel producing much less than the others, an expiring gateway token, Enphase cloud issues or a UPS power cut.
- **Today's curve:** a line chart of production through the day.
- **Panel grid:** all 23 microinverters, shaded by how close each is to its own best output, with the 2 dead ones marked ✕.
- **History:** the last 30 days and 12 months, your best day, CO₂ avoided, and a table view.
- **Placeholders:** "Home use & grid" and "Where the power goes" fill in automatically once the consumption meter and the UPS cable are connected.
- **Auto-refresh:** the page updates every minute while it's open.

**The collector runs on its own.** It's a Windows scheduled task called **Solar Dashboard Collector** that starts hidden when you log in and restarts itself if it crashes. If the PC is off, the dashboard says the gateway is offline and the data pauses.

**Two things for you to do:**
1. **Click "Connect Enphase"** at the bottom of the dashboard and sign in with your **homeowner** account. That brings in your full daily history back to 2021. Until then, the 30-day and 12-month charts only show data from today onward, and today's total only counts since the collector started this afternoon. If Enphase rejects the sign-in with a redirect URL error, add `https://solar-dashboard-coral.vercel.app/api/enphase/callback` to your app in the developer portal. I couldn't check whether the portal needs that.
2. **Get APC's 940-0127 USB cable.** Once it's plugged in, tell me and I'll add the UPS readings to the collector.

The Enphase cloud sync uses about 90 of the 1,000 free API calls a month, and the dashboard stops making calls at 900. The setup steps, the scheduled task and the collector commands are in `solar-dashboard\README.md`. I haven't made a git commit; say the word if you want one or want it on GitHub.

entries.description:
Call this tool to download the content of a Drive file as a base64 encoded string.

If the file is a Google Drive first-party mime type, the `exportMimeType` field specifies the desired export mime type. When the field is unset, defaults to plain text types (e.g. `text/plain`, `text/csv`).

If the file is not found, try using other tools like `search_files` to find the file the user is requesting.

If the user wants a natural language representation of their Drive content, use the `read_file_content` tool (`read_file_content` should be smaller and easier to parse).

exportMimeType.description: Optional. For Google native files, the MIME type to export the file to, ignored otherwise. Defaults to text if not specified.

fileId.description: Required. The ID of the file to retrieve.

revisionId.description: Optional. The revision id for the version of the file to download. If not specified, the latest revision will be downloaded.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Google_Drive__read_file_content
entries.description:
Call this tool to fetch a natural language representation of a known Drive file, and if specified, its comments.

REQUIREMENTS & WORKFLOW:
 - `fileId` is required. You MUST pass an exact Drive file ID returned by a previous discovery tool (`search_files` or `list_recent_files`) or provided explicitly in the user prompt.
 - NEVER guess, invent, or hallucinate a `fileId` string from a file title or name.
 - If given a file title, name, or topic without an explicit `fileId`, you MUST FIRST call `search_files` to find the file and retrieve its `fileId` before invoking this tool.

The file content may be incomplete for very large files. The text representation will change over time, so don't make assumptions about the particular format of the text returned by this tool. If supported and specified, comment tags will be included in the content.

Supported Mime Types:

 - `application/vnd.google-apps.document` (supports comments)
 - `application/vnd.google-apps.presentation` (supports comments)
 - `application/vnd.google-apps.spreadsheet` (supports comments)
 - `application/pdf` 
 - `application/msword` 
 - `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document` 
 - `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet` 
 - `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.presentationml.presentation` 
 - `application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.spreadsheet` 
 - `application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.presentation` 
 - `application/x-vnd.oasis.opendocument.text` 
 - `image/png` 
 - `image/jpeg` 
 - `image/jpg` 

If the file is not found, try using other tools like `search_files` to find the file the user is requesting using keywords.

fileId.description: Required. The ID of the file to retrieve.

includeComments.description: Whether to include comments in the response. Comments will be inlined in the text content of the file with a mapping to the comment threads. Note: Comments are only supported for Google Docs, Slides, and Sheets.

input_schema.description: Request to read file content with support for fetching comments.

content.text:
The readings say **consumption CTs probably aren't connected**.

**What your gateway shows right now**

| | Leg 1 | Leg 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Voltage | 120 V ✅ | 120 V ✅ |
| Current | **0.13 A** | **0.14 A** |

I took five readings over 12 seconds, and they barely moved.

The voltage is real; the gateway measures that through its own wiring. The current is the telling part. Your panels are pushing **5.8 kW** right now, so if consumption CTs were clamped around your main service wires, they'd see a large current, on the order of 10–25 A per leg. That's the solar going out to the grid, or the house pulling in. A steady 0.13 A looks like the background noise of an input with nothing attached.

There's one caveat: the meter is switched off, and I can't be 100% sure a disabled meter reports real current. The deeper CT settings are locked to installer accounts (my request got a 401). So the readings are strong evidence, but not proof.

**How to check for sure, without touching anything live**

Your gateway (part 800-00555, the "metered" model) is usually inside the **IQ Combiner**, a gray box near your main electrical panel or meter.
1. On the gateway's circuit board there are two small terminal blocks labeled **PRODUCTION CT** and **CONSUMPTION CT**.
   - **Wires in CONSUMPTION CT:** the CTs are probably installed and just need enabling.
   - **Empty:** they were never installed.
2. Only look at what you can see without removing panels. If the terminals are behind the inner metal cover (the "dead front"), stop there. Live parts sit behind it, and the main service wires the CTs clamp onto can't be switched off at your breaker.

**What happens next**

| You find | Fix |
|---|---|
| CTs installed, just disabled | They're switched on, and set to the right mode, in Enphase's **installer app**. Homeowner accounts can't do it. Ask Enphase support whether they can enable it remotely, or have the technician do it when they replace your two microinverters. |
| No CTs | The technician installs a pair of Enphase **consumption CTs** (CT-200-SPLIT) around your main service wires, then enables them. It's a short job, but it means working on unfused service conductors, so it's not a DIY task. |

Either way, it fits naturally into the **same visit as the microinverter warranty swap**. Once it's on, the dashboard's "Home use & grid" card and the collector pick it up automatically.

If you can get to the gateway, a photo of its terminal blocks (from a safe distance, no covers removed) is enough for me to tell you which case you're in.

message.content: what should i look for inside the solar panel mox to know if CT is enabled?

content.text:
Quick clarification first: **"enabled" is a software setting, so you can't see it in the box.** We already know from the gateway that it's off. What you *can* see is whether the **CTs are physically installed**, and that decides whether this is a quick setting change or an install job.

**Safety first:** opening the outer door of the box is fine. **Don't remove the inner cover** (the "dead front", the panel the breakers poke through), and don't touch any wiring. The wires the consumption CTs clamp onto stay live even with every breaker off.

### What a CT looks like
A **CT (current transformer)** is a hinged plastic clamp, often black or gray, a bit bigger than a large ring. It snaps around a wire, and two thin wires lead off it, often white and blue or a twisted pair. It usually has an arrow or label on it.

### What to look for

**1. Inside the solar box (IQ Combiner)**
- You should find at least **one CT already**: the **production CT**. It clamps around the wires coming from the solar breakers. Yours works, so it's in there. It shows you what to look for elsewhere.
- Look at the **gateway** (the circuit board, usually at the top, with status lights). If its connection area is visible without removing anything, look for terminal blocks labeled **"PRODUCTION CT"** and **"CONSUMPTION CT"**:
  - **Thin wires in the CONSUMPTION CT terminal:** consumption CTs are almost certainly installed.
  - **CONSUMPTION CT terminal empty:** they were never installed.
- Check the **inside of the door** for labels or stickers. Installers often write "consumption CT" or list the meters there.

**2. Where the consumption CTs would be**
They're **not** on the solar wires. They clamp around the **two thick main service wires**, usually inside your **main electrical panel** right below the meter, sometimes in the meter base. You'd see **two larger clamps**, one on each thick wire, with thin wires running back to the solar box. Don't open the main panel to check; that's the technician's job.

**3. A clue you can check without opening anything**
Look for a **thin wire or small conduit running from the solar box to the main panel**, separate from the big solar wiring. It isn't conclusive, but consumption CT wires have to get from the main panel to the gateway somehow.

### What to tell the technician
| What you saw | Say |
|---|---|
| Wires in the CONSUMPTION CT terminal | "Consumption CTs look installed but the meter is disabled; please enable it, set to *load with solar*, and check the CT direction." |
| Empty terminal or no clamps | "Please install consumption CTs (CT-200-SPLIT) and enable the consumption meter." |

If you take a photo with the outer door open (no covers removed), I'll tell you what I see. If it shows the gateway's terminals, I can usually tell from the photo which case you're in.

content.text:
The photos help, though they can't settle it on their own. Here's what each one shows.

**Photo 1, the outside:** An Eaton **PV AC disconnect** (left) and the Enphase box (right). The thick flexible conduit running down from the disconnect most likely goes to your main panel. That's the route consumption CT wires would take back to the gateway too, so the fact that I can't see a separate small conduit doesn't rule them out.

**Photo 2, inside the box:**
- This is an **IQ Combiner 3**: two 20 A breakers for your two solar circuits (positions 1 and 3), a 10 A **ENVOY** breaker feeding the gateway, and blank slots at 2 and 4.
- The **gateway is mostly hidden behind the black inner cover**. Only its top edge with the status lights shows, so the CT terminals aren't visible. Leave the cover on, as its warning says.
- **The status lights show two red ones.** On these gateways, the middle lights are usually power production and microinverter communication. They turn red when some microinverters aren't producing or reporting, which matches your two dead units. I'd expect them to go green after the replacements.
- The blue **MultiTech** box is an Enphase Mobile Connect **cellular modem**, a backup way for the gateway to reach Enphase. Your gateway is also on your home network, which is how the collector reads it.

**Photo 3, the label inside the door:**
- It confirms the box is an **IQ Combiner 3 (X-IQ-AM1-240-3)** with serial **122025062156**, the same gateway we've been reading.
- The wiring diagram shows a **"Production / Consumption" CT terminal block** on the gateway (P1 for production, C1 and C2 for consumption). It shows one **CT** on the wires going **to PV**. That's the production CT, which comes installed in the box and is the one that's working for you.
- **Consumption CTs aren't drawn in the box.** They're normally a separate add-on (Enphase CT-200-SPLIT) that the installer has to clamp around the main wires in your main electrical panel and run back to C1/C2.

**Putting it together:** the gateway's readings remain the strongest evidence. If consumption CTs were on your mains, they'd see large currents with 5.8 kW of solar flowing, not a steady 0.13 A. Combined with the label showing consumption CTs as an add-on, my best guess is that **they were never installed**. Only someone opening the cover, or looking in your main panel, can confirm it.

**For the technician visit** (microinverters plus metering), ask them to:
1. Check whether anything is wired to the gateway's **C1/C2 consumption terminals**.
2. If not, **install CT-200-SPLIT consumption CTs** on the main service wires and enable the consumption meter as "load with solar."

They might also correct the stickers. The box and conduit are labeled **"DC combiner box" and "DC photovoltaic source circuit,"** but a microinverter system like yours carries **AC** at this point. Firefighters and electricians rely on those labels, so a tech should swap them for accurate ones.

Once the CTs are in, your dashboard's "Home use & grid" card fills in automatically.

message.content: there is a usb c and usb a port oin the front of the apc device. there is also two gigabit ports on the back. why can i not use any of this for connecting?

content.text:
Each of those ports does a different job, and on most APC models only one of them talks to a computer:

| Port | What it's for | Carries UPS data? |
|---|---|---|
| **Front USB-A and USB-C** | **Charging** your phone, tablet and so on. They're power outlets in USB form, and they keep working during an outage. | Usually **no**, power only |
| **Two gigabit ports on the back** (often marked IN / OUT) | **Surge protection for your network cable.** The internet line passes through so a lightning surge doesn't reach your router or PC. | **No.** It's just a protected pass-through for your Ethernet, and the UPS doesn't listen to it. |
| **Data port on the back** (jack-shaped) | **Talking to a computer:** reporting watts, battery level and "on battery" alerts | **Yes, the only one.** It's really a USB port in a jack-shaped socket, so it needs APC's special cable. |

That's why Windows didn't find the UPS. The network cable plus USB-Ethernet adapter turned the data port into a network connection, and the UPS doesn't speak network on that port.

**One thing worth trying:** a few newer APC models do send data over a front USB port. Look at the small label or icon next to the front USB-C:
- A **lightning bolt, battery or "charging"** label means power only.
- A **computer or data icon** means it might work.

content.text:
Yes. ComEd has two free things that are useful here, and one of them can fill the "Home use & grid" gap **without new hardware**.

### 1. Your smart meter usage data
ComEd's smart meters record **15-minute readings** of what you pull from the grid and what your solar sends back. Combined with the solar data the dashboard already has, that gives you home use:

> **home use = solar produced + grid imported − grid exported**

So you'd get the **Home use & grid** card without consumption CTs, with a delay rather than live. There are three ways to get the data:

| Option | How it works | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| **Green Button "Download My Data"** | Log in to your ComEd account and download a file of your 15-minute usage | **Easiest.** Free and works today, but it's manual. I could add an upload box to the dashboard. |
| **Green Button "Connect My Data"** | ComEd's official OAuth API, with data updated daily | Built for companies that register as third parties with ComEd. It may not be practical for one person, but I can look into it. |
| **Live data from the meter itself** | ComEd has said its smart meters can share readings with in-home devices **within about 60 seconds** | Possibly a **live** home-usage feed with no electrician. You'd need a compatible receiver, such as a Zigbee energy-monitor bridge, plus ComEd's approval to pair it. **Ask ComEd whether your meter supports this.** |

### 2. Hourly Pricing API
It's free, public and needs no key. It gives the **electricity price every 5 minutes**:
- `https://hourlypricing.comed.com/api?type=5minutefeed`
- `https://hourlypricing.comed.com/api?type=currenthouraverage`

This matters most if you're on **ComEd's Hourly Pricing plan**. Then the dashboard could show what your solar is worth right now, or flag good times to run the dishwasher or dryer. On a standard fixed rate, the dashboard could instead use your plan's rate to estimate savings.

### My suggestion
1. **Now:** download your **Green Button data** from your ComEd account (look for "Green Button" or "Download My Data" under usage), save it into the `solar-photos` folder or anywhere on your PC, and I'll build the home-use and grid view from it.
2. **Ask ComEd** whether your smart meter can pair with an in-home device for live data. If it can, that's the cheapest route to live home usage. The consumption CTs from the technician visit would still be the most direct option.

Do you know whether you're on ComEd's Hourly Pricing plan or a standard fixed rate?

This file has ComEd's **billing totals**: net kWh and cost per billing period from Sept 2023 to Sept 2026. It isn't the 15-minute detail, but combined with your solar history it shows **how much your house actually used**. The calculation is grid net + solar produced, and every day in those periods had solar data, so nothing was guessed.

### Something big changed around February–March 2026

| Billing period | 2025: home used | 2026: home used | Change | 2025 bill | 2026 bill |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Feb–Mar | 821 kWh | 1,348 kWh | **+64%** | $19.75 | $112.56 |
| Mar–Apr | 784 | 1,575 | **+101%** | $19.71 | $113.70 |
| Apr–May | 1,163 | 1,540 | +32% | $19.69 | $122.94 |
| May–Jun | 844 | 1,793 | **+112%** | $19.75 | $137.59 |
| Jun–Jul | 1,706 | 2,358 | +38% | $33.47 | $223.75 |
| Jul–Aug | 1,506 | 1,938 | +29% | $91.63 | $212.24 |
| Aug–Sep | 1,316 | 2,493 | **+89%** | $46.12 | $270.48 |

**Your solar isn't the main cause.** Production in 2026 is close to 2025 (about 1,000–1,200 kWh in the sunny months). July 2026 dipped to 868 kWh, which fits with the second microinverter dying on July 23. But the panels lost maybe 10%, while **the house is using roughly 50–100% more electricity.**

The spring months are the clearest clue. March–April needs almost no heating or AC, yet usage roughly doubled: about **+26 kWh a day**, the same as something drawing **about 1 kW around the clock**. A few things fit that pattern:
- a computer, server or mining rig running 24/7
- an electric space heater, dehumidifier or hot tub
- an EV or e-bike charged regularly
- a failing appliance running nonstop, such as an old fridge or freezer, a sump or well pump, or an AC or heat pump that won't shut off

**Did anything new arrive or change around February 2026?**

### Next steps
1. **Download ComEd's interval data** (the 15-minute usage, not billing). It's on the same Green Button page; choose usage or interval data instead of billing. The **overnight hours** in that data would show whether the extra load is always on, which points to a device, or concentrated at certain times, which points to a habit or appliance cycle.
2. **The UPS reading will help.** Once the APC cable is in, we'll know exactly what your desk setup draws around the clock.
3. **I can add this to the dashboard** as a **"Home use by billing period"** chart (solar vs grid vs total, with cost) in the Home use & grid card. It would fill that card with real numbers until live metering is possible.

**What changed on https://solar-dashboard-coral.vercel.app:**

**"Home use & grid" now has real numbers.** Since live metering isn't available, it uses each billing period: home use = ComEd net kWh + the solar your panels produced over the same dates.
- **Latest bill (Aug 19 – Sep 20, 2026):** **$270.48**, **2,493 kWh** used, **76 kWh/day**, **+72% vs last year**, and **41%** covered by solar.
- **A chart of all 36 billing periods** since Sept 2023, with the latest highlighted. Hover over any bar for the solar/grid split and the bill.
- **A table view** with each period's solar, grid, home use, change from last year and cost.

**New warning in Problems: "Home electricity use is up 72% on last year."** That's 76 kWh/day vs 44 a year earlier ($270.48 vs $46.12), while solar output is about the same. The comparison is per day, so billing periods of different lengths don't skew it. This warning updates whenever you import a new bill, and it goes away if usage drops back to within 30% of the previous year.

**To add future bills:** download the new billing CSV and run the one-line import command in the README, or just tell me it's in Downloads.

The rise starting around **February–March 2026** is the most important thing the data shows. It works out to roughly 1 kW running around the clock. If anything new arrived around then, or you'd like to dig in, ComEd's **15-minute interval** download would show whether the extra load runs all night or only at certain times. That's usually enough to identify the culprit.

content.text:
That explains most of it. With two more people in the house, a big jump is expected.

**Is +72% about right for two extra people?** It's on the high side, but plausible. Rough figures for each person added:
- **Hot water** (showers and laundry), if your water heater is electric: about 3–6 kWh/day each. Usually the biggest piece.
- **Laundry and dryer:** about 1–3 kWh/day more.
- **Cooking, dishwasher, lights:** about 1–2 kWh/day each.
- **Computers, TVs, chargers**, especially if they work or game from home: about 1–5 kWh/day each.
- **Heating and cooling more rooms more of the time**, or a **space heater or window AC** in a bedroom. That can be large: 1 kW running 10 hours is 10 kWh/day.

Two people commonly add about **10–25 kWh/day**. You're up about **32 kWh/day** compared with last year, so most of it is explained, possibly with one bigger item on top, like a space heater, a gaming PC left on, an electric car or bike, or a mini-fridge. That's worth a quick look, but nothing seems broken.

**I'd adjust the dashboard to match.** Right now it calls this a problem, which it isn't. I can:
- Show **kWh per person per day** next to the totals, so comparisons stay fair as the household changes.
- Only warn if **per-person** usage jumps, so it catches something new running nonstop, not normal life with more people.
- Mark the move-in date on the billing chart.

For that I need two things:
1. **How many people lived there before?**
2. **About when did the two new people move in?** The month is enough. The data suggests around February 2026.

I found Home Assistant at **192.168.1.107:8123**. Its API is up and asking for a login, which is normal. Once I have a token, I can see every power and energy sensor it tracks: smart plugs, an energy monitor, or an Enphase integration it may already have. The collector can then send those readings to your dashboard every minute.

**To create the token (about one minute):**
1. Open Home Assistant in your browser.
2. Click **your name or profile picture** at the bottom-left of the sidebar.
3. Open the **Security** tab and scroll to **Long-lived access tokens**.
4. Click **Create token** and name it something like `solar-dashboard`.
5. Copy the token; Home Assistant shows it only once.
6. Paste it into `solar-dashboard\collector\.env` after `HA_TOKEN=`. I've already added that line, with the address filled in. Save the file.

As with the gateway token, put it in the file, not in chat. The token has the same access as your Home Assistant account, but the collector only **reads** sensor values; it never turns anything on or off. For extra safety, create a separate **non-admin user** in Home Assistant (Settings → People) just for this, and make the token from that user.

Tell me when it's saved. I'll list your power sensors, and then you can choose which ones go into "Where the power goes."

content.text:
Home Assistant connected fine and can see 110 devices and entities, **but none of them measure real power use.** Here's what's there:

| What Home Assistant has | Power data? |
|---|---|
| **2 WLED light strips** ("Dungeon Strip", "CLOUDS") | Only an *estimated* current of about 0.5 A each. At typical 5 V strip voltage that's roughly **3 W apiece**. |
| Govee light bar, LIFX, a candle light | On/off and color only |
| **Range** (via SmartThings) | Oven state and temperature, no wattage |
| TVs and media players (Google TV, Vizio, LG, Chromecast, displays) | Playing or off, no wattage |
| Blink camera, phone, Raspberry Pi | Battery and status only |

So for now, Home Assistant can't tell us where the extra ~32 kWh a day is going.

**It's still the easiest place to add measurement.** Home Assistant already supports **Matter**, **SmartThings** and HACS integrations, so any **smart plug with energy monitoring** you add will show up automatically. A few that work well with it:
- **Shelly Plug US** (Wi-Fi): native Home Assistant support, fully local, very accurate.
- **TP-Link Tapo P110M** or **Eve Energy** (Matter): add them in Home Assistant from the Matter screen.

Put them on the things you suspect: **space heaters, the PCs or gaming setups, a mini-fridge, the TV area, any dehumidifier or window AC.** A big hardwired appliance needs a circuit monitor instead; a plug can't measure it.

**I can wire this up now** so it's ready when plugs arrive. The collector would read every Home Assistant sensor that reports **watts**, and the "Where the power goes" card would rank them live, alongside the UPS once its cable arrives. Until then the card would stay empty. **Should I build it?**

I'm also still waiting on two answers for the per-person view: **how many people lived there before**, and **roughly which month the two new people moved in**.

content.text:
The new **"Where the power goes"** section is live at https://solar-dashboard-coral.vercel.app, and the collector is reading Home Assistant every minute. The collector log shows it pushing readings after the restart.

It's empty for now because none of your Home Assistant devices report watts yet. It will fill in as soon as one does. I checked how it looks by temporarily filling it with made-up sample devices on my own machine; that sample data never went to your real dashboard.

**What it shows once devices report watts:**
- **Totals:** watts in use now, kWh today, the estimated monthly cost of everything measured, and what share of a typical day's use (76 kWh, from your latest bill) the measured devices account for.
- **A device ranking**, biggest energy user first, with its room, kWh per day, watts right now, and cost per month. The cost uses about **$0.19/kWh**, worked out from your ComEd bills.
- **A room ranking** that groups devices by the rooms you've set in Home Assistant (Living Room, Kitchen, Bedroom).
- **Averages:** each device's daily use averages over the last 7 days. Until a full day is recorded, it projects from today's pace and says so.

**To start using it:** add energy-monitoring smart plugs (Shelly Plug US, Tapo P110M or Eve Energy) to Home Assistant and assign each to a room. They'll appear within a minute, with no code changes.

**About the two copper connectors on the back of the UPS:** they're almost certainly **coax "IN / OUT" connectors**, the threaded brass-colored kind used for cable TV or cable internet. Like the gigabit ports, they're **surge protection** for the coax line between the wall and your modem or TV box. They don't carry any UPS data. If yours is a single screw rather than a threaded pair, it's a **ground screw** for bonding other equipment, which also carries no data. The **data port with APC's 940-0127 cable** is still the only way to read the UPS.

content.text:
No, it works from anywhere. **https://solar-dashboard-coral.vercel.app** is on Vercel's servers on the public internet, so you can open it from your phone on cellular, at work or while traveling. Anyone who has the link still needs your **dashboard password**.

What *is* local is the **collector**, the small program on your home PC. It reads the gateway and Home Assistant over your home network and sends readings to the website every minute.

| Part | Where it runs | Works away from home? |
|---|---|---|
| The dashboard website | Vercel (internet) | ✅ Yes, any device with the password |
| Enphase cloud history (daily totals since 2021, bills) | Vercel + Enphase cloud | ✅ Always, even if your PC is off |
| Live data (watts now, per-panel, today's curve, devices) | Collector on your home PC | ✅ You can *view* it anywhere, but it only updates while the home PC is on |

**If the home PC is off or asleep**, the page shows "Gateway offline" and a Problems entry saying the collector is offline. History and totals stay visible. Live readings resume as soon as the PC is back on.

Two tips:

content.text:
Partly. There's no feed of your actual neighbors' usage, since utilities keep individual homes private, but you can get close in a few ways:

### Electricity use: how your home compares
| Source | What you get | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| **Your ComEd online account** | ComEd's home energy reports usually include a **"compare to similar nearby homes"** chart: similar size, same area, and "efficient neighbors." It's the closest thing to a real neighborhood comparison. | Just look; there's no API, so I can't pull it in automatically |
| **Government averages (EIA)** | Average monthly kWh for **Illinois homes** and the US, updated monthly. It's a free API. | Easy for me to add to the Home use chart as a "typical Illinois home" line |
| **ComEd anonymized area data** | ComEd has offered **anonymized, aggregated usage by ZIP code** for research | Requires a request through ComEd; worth asking, but not instant |

### Solar: is your system performing as well as it should?
| Source | What you get | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| **NREL PVWatts** (free government API) | **Expected** production for an 8.05 kW system at your location, with typical weather, per month. It tells you whether your panels are underperforming beyond the two dead microinverters. | Easy to add: an "expected vs actual" line on the 12-month chart. It needs only your **approximate** location (town level) and roof direction and tilt. |
| **PVOutput.org** | A free community site where solar owners share production. You can compare against **real systems nearby**. | You'd make a free account, and the collector can upload your data. Your production would then be visible on their site, so it's optional. |

### My suggestion
1. **Check ComEd's "similar homes" comparison in your account.** It's the only true neighbor comparison, and it'll show whether your 76 kWh/day is unusual for your area.
2. **I'll add two benchmarks to the dashboard:**
   - an **"Average Illinois home"** reference on the home-use chart (EIA)
   - **"Expected production" vs actual** on the solar charts (PVWatts)

For PVWatts I need your roof's **direction** (south, southwest and so on) and roughly how steep it is (low, medium or steep is enough). I'd use only the town-level location, never your address. Should I go ahead?

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding PVWatts API v8 and the domain migration:

## Domain Migration to developer.nlr.gov

Existing API users need to update any developer.nrel.gov references in their code to developer.nlr.gov, as the previous developer.nrel.gov domain was retired on May 29, 2026. The previous domain experienced scheduled service disruptions beginning May 1, 2026, before being shut down on May 29, 2026.

## PVWatts API v8 Details

Version 8 of the PVWatts Calculator web API became available as of November 14, 2022, adding a bifacial module option, a new input for monthly irradiance losses, new inputs for specifying albedo, and updating the photovoltaic module, inverter, and thermal effects models to use more detailed and industry-accepted algorithms.

PVWatts V8 also updates the weather data to 2020 TMY data from the National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB) for locations covered by the database.

The new documentation is now available at **developer.nlr.gov** instead of the previous developer.nrel.gov domain.
